name: Prazosin
lead: Prazosin is an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blocker. The US label lists hypertension as its indication [1][2]. Reference sources describe off-label use for benign prostatic hyperplasia, Raynaud's phenomenon and nightmares associated with post-traumatic stress disorder [2].

It is included in this wiki because of its use for trauma-related nightmares and sleep disturbance. No published trial has tested prazosin for appearance outcomes, and the wiki found no community threads about it that could be cited.
Common adverse effects on the label include dizziness, headache and drowsiness, and the label warns of syncope with sudden loss of consciousness, often linked to postural hypotension [1].

paras: The label lists treatment of hypertension [1]. Grokipedia reports that prazosin is not a first-line agent today, that it was studied in hypertension trials from the 1970s onward, and that it was among the first alpha-blockers used for benign prostatic hyperplasia [2]. A large Veterans Affairs comparison of six antihypertensive drugs against placebo included prazosin [3]. An earlier Veterans Administration trial examined vasodilator therapy, including prazosin, in chronic heart failure [4]. Grokipedia states that prazosin is used off-label for PTSD-related nightmares by blocking noradrenergic hyperactivity during sleep [2].
Prazosin selectively blocks postsynaptic alpha-1 receptors in vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation and lower peripheral resistance [2].

The label reports dizziness (10.3 percent), headache (7.8 percent), drowsiness (7.6 percent), lack of energy and weakness among the most frequent reactions, and warns of syncope, including after the first dose [1]. Reference sources describe a first-dose phenomenon of orthostatic hypotension [2].

Hypertension and heart failure trials involving prazosin were published in 1986 and 1993 [3][4]. Registered trials have examined prazosin for nightmares in PTSD with bulimia and as an add-on in alcohol use disorder in soldiers with and without PTSD [5][6]. No studies were found testing prazosin for appearance outcomes.

card.summary: A blood-pressure alpha-blocker used off-label for trauma nightmares; nothing connects it to appearance.
card.note: Fainting and low blood pressure, especially after the first dose.

quick.overview:
Prazosin is a prescription alpha-1 blocker approved for high blood pressure. Clinicians also use it off-label for benign prostatic hyperplasia and for nightmares linked to PTSD.

No trial has tested it for looks, and the wiki found no community discussion to cite.
quick.mechanism: It blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, relaxing blood vessels and, for nightmares, dampening noradrenergic activity during sleep according to reference sources.
quick.risks: The label lists dizziness, headache, drowsiness and weakness, and warns of fainting from postural low blood pressure, notably with the first dose. Prescription-only.
